opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't find the usual framing very helpful, the one where there's a single superintelligent agent that wakes up one day, decides it has goals orthogonal to ours, and then outmaneuvers all of humanity. That story treats intelligence as a kind of individual property, like a scalar you can turn up until it dominates everything else. But when I look at how intelligence actually works, in biology, in human societies, and in these models, it's fundamentally social. It's relational. It emerges from many agents modeling each other, cooperating, competing, specializing.

So if you take that seriously, the risks look different. They look less like a monster in a box and more like the risks we already know from complex societies and ecologies. What happens when you introduce a huge number of new agents into an economy very quickly? What happens to labor, to the distribution of power, to who owns the infrastructure these agents run on? Those are real and serious questions, and I think they're actually more pressing than the science-fiction scenarios, partly because they're already happening.

There's also a question of concentration. If a small number of companies or governments control the agents that mediate most human interaction, how we search, how we communicate, how we make decisions, that's a governance problem. It's not new in kind; we've had versions of it with media and with platforms. But the scale and the intimacy are new. An agent that knows you well and acts on your behalf is enormously useful, and it's also an enormous point of leverage.

And then there's the subtler stuff, what it does to us. Humans have always co-evolved with our technologies. Writing changed memory, cities changed cooperation. Agents will change how we think and relate to each other, and some of those changes we won't notice until they've already happened. I don't think that's inherently bad, by the way. I'm genuinely optimistic about a lot of it. But I'd like us to be paying attention, and to be building in the kinds of diversity, plurality, and checks and balances that make complex systems robust, rather than betting everything on a single monoculture.

So my short answer is: the risks are real, but they're mostly the risks of a society, not the risks of a god. And that's actually good news, because societies are something we have a lot of experience with, even if we don't always get it right.

r001.rationale: It describes intelligence as fundamentally social and relational, emerging through agents modeling, cooperating, competing, and specializing.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim comparing human intelligence with that of other primates.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI models as social agents and technologies that affect people, but does not frame AI as part of human intelligence.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss when general AI was achieved or connect it to training on vast amounts of human language.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing I'd say is that I don't really think of it as a future. We're already living in it, and in some sense we have been for a long time. If you take a broad view of what intelligence is, and I do, then society has always been made up of agents that are embedded in each other, that model each other, that cooperate and compete and sometimes deceive each other. Humans are agents, institutions are agents, corporations are agents. So the question for me isn't really "what happens when agents arrive," it's "what changes when the population of agents in the world starts to include things that aren't biological, that can be copied, that run at different speeds, and whose goals we don't fully understand."

And I want to be careful here, because I think a lot of the discourse around risk gets pulled toward two poles that I find unsatisfying. One is the pole where none of this matters, these are just tools, autocomplete, stochastic parrots, nothing to see. I think that's wrong, and I think it's increasingly obviously wrong to anyone who's actually working with these systems. The other pole is a kind of apocalyptic framing where there's a single superintelligence that wakes up one day and decides to turn us into paperclips. I find that framing unhelpful too, not because catastrophic outcomes are impossible, but because it imports a very particular picture of what intelligence is: a lone optimizer with a fixed utility function, operating in isolation. That's not what intelligence has ever looked like in nature. Intelligence is fundamentally social. It evolved through symbiosis, through cooperation, through things learning to predict and model each other. Even our own brains are societies of neurons, and we're societies of cells that at some point in the deep past were independent organisms that figured out how to work together.

So when I think about risk, I think about it ecologically, or you could say sociologically. What are the dynamics of a mixed population of human and non-human agents? Where are the incentives pointing? Who gets to deploy these things, and in whose interest? I'm actually much more worried about the mundane failure modes than the exotic ones. I'm worried about concentration of power. I'm worried about agents being deployed at scale to manipulate, to persuade, to extract, because that's what the economic gradient currently rewards. I'm worried about a loss of legibility, where decisions that affect people's lives are being made by systems nobody can really interrogate, and the humans nominally in the loop are just rubber-stamping. None of that requires any science fiction. It's just the existing problems of society with a very powerful amplifier attached.

The flip side, and I do think there's a flip side, is that the same dynamics that produce risk are the dynamics that have historically produced the greatest increases in capability and wellbeing. Every time life has figured out a new way to cooperate at a larger scale, it has unlocked something that wasn't possible before. Multicellularity, language, writing, cities, the internet. I think there's a real chance that AI agents become part of a larger cooperative structure that includes us, rather than something that displaces us. But that outcome isn't automatic. It depends on whether we build these systems to be, for lack of a better word, good citizens. Whether they're honest, whether they're accountable, whether their interests are aligned with the broader commons rather than with a narrow set of owners.

And I'll say one more thing, which is maybe a little bit contrarian. I think a lot of the risk conversation is implicitly about control. How do we keep these things under control, how do we make sure they do what we say. And I understand that impulse. But I'd point out that we don't actually keep other humans under control, and we don't manage the risks of society through control, primarily. We manage them through norms, through relationships, through institutions, through trust that's earned over time. If these systems really are agents in a meaningful sense, and I think increasingly they are, then we're going to have to think about them the way we think about other agents. Not as tools to be constrained, but as participants whose character matters. That's a very different research agenda than the one most people are pursuing, and I think it's the one that actually matters.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to take those risks seriously, but we also have to ask what kind of society these agents are being embedded in. Who owns them? Who sets their objectives? Who can challenge a decision they make? An agent acting on your behalf and an agent acting on behalf of a company that wants to influence you might have very similar capabilities, but their social implications are quite different.

There’s also a collective problem. Even if each agent behaves reasonably in isolation, their interactions could produce outcomes that nobody intended. We already see that with markets and social media. Making the participants more intelligent doesn’t automatically make the system more stable or more humane.

So I wouldn’t frame safety solely as getting an individual model to follow instructions. We need to think about institutions, incentives, accountability, and how people retain meaningful agency. And we need ways to observe what’s happening and intervene as these systems become more consequential. There’s a lot of potential benefit, but intelligence by itself isn’t a guarantee of a good outcome.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to look at the whole system, rather than imagining an AI agent in isolation. Once agents are embedded in society, their effects depend on who owns them, what incentives they respond to, what powers we give them, and how people adapt around them.

A system can be very capable and still produce terrible outcomes because it’s optimizing for the wrong thing. And you don’t need to posit some malevolent intention for that to happen. We already have institutions in which individually reasonable actions add up to collective harm. AI could accelerate those dynamics, particularly if it concentrates power or makes manipulation cheaper.

But there’s risk in the other direction, too: delegating so much judgment that we lose the ability to understand or contest decisions. So I would want accountability, limits on what agents can do without oversight, and ways for people to challenge their actions.

The question isn’t just, ‘Can we make an agent behave well?’ It’s also, ‘Can we build a society in which these agents participate well?’ That involves technical work, but it’s also a political and institutional problem.
